paragraphs: This paper studies how a network of agents can agree on a decision while each agent has its own objective and constraints. Communication is restricted: two agents can exchange information directly only when an edge connects them. The shared goal is to minimize the sum of their individual convex objectives, while choosing a decision that satisfies every agent’s private conic constraints.

The proposed primal-dual approach addresses optimization and coordination together. A decision can be attractive according to the combined objective yet violate someone’s constraints, and different agents can hold inconsistent decisions. The paper therefore provides convergence rates for three separate quantities: distance from the optimal objective value, constraint infeasibility, and disagreement among agents.

The analysis also examines how the network’s connection pattern affects convergence. This links the mathematical guarantees to the communication structure through which cooperation must occur. Finally, the authors explain how to extend the decentralized methods to networks whose connections change over time, broadening the setting beyond a fixed communication graph.
neurips-2016-a-primal-dual-method-for-co.tldr: A decentralized primal-dual method coordinates convex optimization under private conic constraints, with convergence guarantees covering accuracy, feasibility, and agreement.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical framework for learning the parameters of sum-product networks. Its starting point is a structural result: any network satisfying completeness and decomposability is equivalent to a mixture of trees, with each tree representing a product of distributions over individual variables. This gives parameter learning a mixture-model interpretation.

Using that interpretation, the authors characterize maximum-likelihood learning and express its optimization problem as a signomial program. They then derive two algorithms, one based on sequential monomial approximations and the other on the concave-convex procedure. Both naturally produce multiplicative parameter updates, avoiding a separate projection operation during optimization.

The framework also reveals a precise connection between two learning procedures. For these networks, the concave-convex procedure yields the same algorithm as expectation maximization, although the procedures differ in general. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and explanatory: it supplies update methods while showing how seemingly distinct approaches arise from a shared view of the model.
neurips-2016-a-unified-approach-for-lear.tldr: A mixture-of-trees interpretation unifies sum-product network parameter learning and connects multiplicative optimization updates with expectation maximization.

paragraphs: The stochastic block model describes networks with underlying communities and provides a mathematical setting for studying community detection. Its detection problem exhibits thresholds that separate different levels of recoverable community information. This paper addresses whether an efficient algorithm can reach the Kesten-Stigum threshold, a conjecture previously proved for two symmetric communities but still open for three or more.

The authors prove the conjecture and obtain a broader result for arbitrary stochastic block models whose communities have sizes proportional to the network size. Their method is linearized acyclic belief propagation. It reduces the effects of cycles in the graph while achieving the threshold with a running time of O(n ln n).

The paper also connects this message-passing algorithm to power iteration on a generalized nonbacktracking operator. That connection gives a formal relationship between spectral calculations and message passing. Together, the results expand the models covered by an efficient threshold guarantee while preserving or improving the computational complexity of earlier approaches.
neurips-2016-achieving-the-ks-threshold-.tldr: Linearized acyclic belief propagation achieves the Kesten-Stigum detection threshold in O(n ln n) time for stochastic block models with linear-size communities.

paragraphs: Binary hashing represents data using short sequences of bits so that approximate nearest-neighbor search can be fast. Learning useful codes requires preserving neighborhood relationships while making the bits sufficiently different from one another. Existing approaches often enforce this diversity through constraints or penalties that tie the hash functions together, making their optimization harder.

The paper proposes training each hash function independently and introducing diversity through techniques borrowed from classifier ensembles. Each bit can therefore be learned without jointly optimizing all the other bits. This separates the work across hash functions and makes the training process straightforward to parallelize, while still addressing the need for varied contributions to the final code.

In image-retrieval experiments, the authors report that this simpler strategy is faster and improves on a more complex coupled objective. They also report state-of-the-art precision and recall. These findings support independent training with ensemble diversity as an effective alternative to enforcing relationships among bits inside a single difficult optimization problem.
neurips-2016-an-ensemble-diversity-appro.tldr: Training hash bits independently with ensemble-inspired diversity improves speed and image-retrieval performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Robots and autonomous vehicles need to infer hidden states from streams of sensor observations. Probabilistic filters and smoothers are widely used for this task, but generative approaches must describe the distribution of sensor readings. Rich inputs such as camera images make that modeling requirement demanding. Discriminative approaches avoid that requirement, although training them with hidden states can be complicated.

The paper treats the parameters of the estimated state distribution as outputs of a deterministic computation graph. This makes it possible to train the estimator directly with gradient descent. The graph can include expressive nonlinear components, such as convolutional neural networks, to process raw images before contributing to state estimation.

The resulting model can be understood as a recurrent neural network whose architecture draws on probabilistic filtering. Evaluations use a synthetic tracking task with raw images and visual odometry on KITTI. The reported improvements over standard generative approaches and ordinary recurrent networks suggest that filtering structure can be useful when learning state estimators from complex observations.
neurips-2016-backprop-kf-learning-discri.tldr: Backprop KF trains image-based state estimators through a deterministic computation graph that combines neural processing with probabilistic filtering structure.

paragraphs: Groups of neurons differ in their types, locations, connectivity, and responses. This paper asks how such hidden organization can be inferred from simultaneously recorded spike trains. The authors argue that conventional clustering and dimensionality-reduction methods are poorly matched to this problem because they do not adequately use temporal dependencies or account for noise in the recordings.

Their approach extends a multi-neuron point-process generalized linear model into a hierarchical model. Flexible graph-based priors connect hidden neuronal features with patterns of connectivity. This makes temporal activity and circuit organization parts of the same inference problem, rather than treating the recorded activity only as material for a separate clustering step.

The authors perform fully Bayesian inference using Pólya-gamma augmentation. The resulting method can classify neurons and infer latent dimensions of circuit organization from correlated spike trains. Applications to synthetic data and primate-retina recordings reveal patterns associated with neural types and locations using spike recordings alone, demonstrating the approach’s ability to recover meaningful hidden structure in those settings.
neurips-2016-bayesian-latent-structure-d.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model infers latent neural types and locations from spike trains by linking temporal activity with connectivity structure.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems must predict ratings for user–movie pairs that have not been observed. This paper models each rating as a noisy value of an unknown function of user and movie features. The distinctive difficulty is that those features are also hidden. The authors call this blind regression because the inputs normally available to a regression method are missing.

Drawing inspiration from Taylor expansion, they derive a prediction algorithm that is consistent for Lipschitz functions. The analysis leads naturally to a variant of collaborative filtering, giving that familiar recommendation strategy a nonparametric interpretation. It connects predictions based on other observed ratings with an underlying function whose inputs need not be explicitly recovered.

The error guarantee assumes independent sampling with probability at least max(m^(-1+δ), n^(-1/2+δ)), where δ is positive. Under this condition, the expected fraction of errors exceeding ε is bounded by the additive-noise variance divided by ε², plus a polynomially decreasing term. MovieLens and Netflix experiments suggest improvements over basic collaborative filtering and competitiveness with matrix factorization.
neurips-2016-blind-regression-nonparamet.tldr: Blind regression gives collaborative filtering a nonparametric foundation for predicting missing ratings when both user and item features are hidden.

paragraphs: Human pose estimation involves predicting related body joints, so the structure connecting those predictions matters. This paper combines convolutional neural networks with a probabilistic framework for representing that structure. Its motivation is that a classical neural network does not pass messages between neurons within the same layer, limiting that particular route for exchanging information among joint representations.

The proposed CRF-CNN models structural relationships in both hidden feature layers and the output layer. Its message-passing scheme allows each body joint to receive information from all the others at multiple layers. Thus, relationships among joints can influence the internal features used for prediction as well as the final joint estimates.

The authors implement message passing through convolutions between feature maps in the same layer and integrate it with ordinary forward propagation. This yields a neural-network implementation that can be trained end to end. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, supporting the value of incorporating structured interactions throughout the pose-estimation network.
neurips-2016-crf-cnn-modeling-structured.tldr: CRF-CNN improves structured human pose modeling by passing messages among body-joint representations in hidden layers and outputs.

paragraphs: Recognizing actions in video requires context as well as local visual features. This paper argues for collecting that context early in feature learning and preserving how it develops across the hierarchy. The motivation is that waiting until hierarchical local features have already been extracted can overlook contextual evolution that helps distinguish similar actions.

The proposed deep alternative neural network stacks layers that pair volumetric convolution with recurrence. The convolutional component learns local features, while the recurrent component gathers context. Repeating this arrangement lets contextual information participate from the beginning and continue through successive levels of representation. The authors show that these hierarchical contextual changes are essential to recognizing similar actions in their study.

The system also adapts the temporal extent of its input using optical-flow energy and introduces volumetric pyramid pooling to handle clips of arbitrary sizes. Results on HMDB51 and UCF101 are competitive with or superior to state-of-the-art methods. These evaluations support both the architecture and its emphasis on early, evolving context.
neurips-2016-deep-alternative-neural-net.tldr: DANN alternates volumetric convolution and recurrence to capture context early and preserve its evolution for video action recognition.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a criterion for assessing discrimination in supervised prediction with respect to a specified sensitive attribute. The setting is a learned system that predicts a target from available features. The criterion gives the authors a defined standard against which a predictor can be evaluated and adjusted, making the intended meaning of removing discrimination explicit within their framework.

The central result is a way to optimally adjust any learned predictor so that it satisfies this standard. The result assumes access to data about the predictor, the target, and membership in the protected group. Those information requirements are part of the setting in which the adjustment is established, and the guarantee concerns discrimination according to the proposed definition.

The framework also changes who bears the cost of poor classification. The authors argue that it shifts that burden from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker. Improving predictive accuracy then becomes a way for the decision maker to respond, connecting the fairness requirement with incentives to improve the underlying classifier.
neurips-2016-equality-of-opportunity-in-.tldr: The paper defines a discrimination criterion and shows how to optimally adjust learned predictors to satisfy it under stated data-access assumptions.

paragraphs: Some statistical models are easy to simulate but have likelihoods that are impractical to evaluate. Approximate Bayesian Computation addresses this by accepting simulated data sufficiently close to the observations. The closeness tolerance, ε, creates a tradeoff: shrinking it improves the approximation, but greatly slows sampling. With a finite tolerance, these methods typically sample a distribution broader than the desired posterior.

This paper replaces that tolerance-based approach with Bayesian conditional density estimation. It learns a parametric representation of the posterior from simulations. Preliminary inference using a limited amount of simulated data guides subsequent simulations, so the process uses what it has already learned to decide where further simulation effort should go.

The reported efficiency advantage can be substantial: in some cases, learning an accurate representation of the entire true posterior requires fewer simulations than Monte Carlo ABC needs for one sample from an approximate posterior. That comparison is explicitly case-dependent. It highlights the potential benefit of learning a reusable posterior distribution while directing simulations through successive rounds of inference.
neurips-2016-fast-free-inference-of-simu.tldr: Bayesian conditional density estimation learns simulation-model posteriors without an ε acceptance threshold and uses preliminary inference to guide further simulations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a topic model that connects spatial brain activity with language describing cognitive function. In its neuroimaging application, a topic represents a functional brain region through two linked probability distributions: one describes the region’s spatial extent, and the other describes associated linguistic terms. This provides a joint representation of where activity occurs and what function it is associated with.

Generalized Correspondence-LDA extends the earlier correspondence model in two ways. It permits different spatial representations for topics and allows more flexibility in how strongly the data types correspond. The authors present three variants, each with a different spatial representation, and apply them to a corpus of neuroimaging data.

The reported findings include qualitative improvements in the kinds of topics recovered when alternative spatial representations are used. The model can also incorporate prior knowledge from neuroimaging research. Its new features improve predictions of missing data, giving a predictive result alongside the qualitative evidence that more flexible spatial and cross-data modeling produces useful representations.
neurips-2016-generalized-correspondence-.tldr: GC-LDA links brain-activity locations with cognitive language using flexible spatial topics and improves missing-data prediction.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains representations for comparing examples. The paper identifies a weakness in common contrastive and triplet-loss approaches: an update often uses only one negative example, leaving other negative classes out of that comparison. The authors describe this limited interaction as one contributor to slow convergence.

Their multi-class N-pair loss generalizes triplet loss by comparing against N−1 negative examples jointly. This gives each update information about several competing classes. The paper also introduces a batch-construction strategy that uses only N pairs of examples instead of (N+1)×N examples, reducing the work required to compute deep embeddings for these comparisons.

The authors report better results than triplet loss and other competing objectives across several visual-recognition benchmarks. The tasks include fine-grained recognition and verification, image clustering and retrieval, and face verification and identification. These findings support the usefulness of considering multiple negative classes together, while the batch strategy addresses the computational burden that would otherwise accompany richer comparisons.
neurips-2016-improved-deep-metric-learni.tldr: Multi-class N-pair loss compares several negative classes per update and uses efficient batches to improve deep metric learning.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can learn representations without labels, but adding multiple dependent stochastic layers makes training difficult. This limits the benefit of their increased expressive capacity. The Ladder Variational Autoencoder addresses the inference side of that problem: how observations are used to estimate the hidden variables in a deep generative model.

Its inference procedure recursively corrects the generative distribution using a data-dependent approximate likelihood. The process resembles the Ladder Network and differs from inference that proceeds purely from the input upward. By combining the generative distribution with observation-dependent corrections, the method provides a different way to use the hierarchy during inference.

The authors report state-of-the-art predictive log-likelihood and a tighter likelihood lower bound compared with bottom-up layered variational autoencoders and other generative models. Their representation analysis finds a deeper, more distributed use of latent variables. They also observe that batch normalization and gradually introducing the KL term are crucial for training models with many stochastic layers, tying the reported success to both inference design and training procedure.
neurips-2016-ladder-variational-autoenco.tldr: Ladder Variational Autoencoders recursively combine generative structure with data-dependent corrections to train deeper, more distributed latent hierarchies.

paragraphs: Translating natural-language requests into programs requires identifying which words specify the relevant program elements. This paper focuses on the restricted but useful task of producing If-Then programs from textual descriptions. It introduces a neural architecture trained end to end, with an attention mechanism designed to make better use of the structure in those descriptions.

Latent Attention assigns multiplicative weights to words through a two-stage process. The purpose is to identify the parts of the description that matter for predicting particular program elements. The resulting architecture reduces the error rate by 28.57% compared with prior work, providing the paper’s main reported improvement for the standard synthesis setting.

The authors also introduce a one-shot learning scenario and simulate it using their existing dataset. They modify the training procedure for this scenario and find that the variation outperforms the original procedure. It significantly narrows the gap to a model trained on all available data, indicating that training design can help the architecture work in the proposed limited-example setting.
neurips-2016-latent-attention-for-if-the.tldr: Two-stage Latent Attention improves translation from text to If-Then programs, with an adapted training procedure also helping in a simulated one-shot setting.

paragraphs: Learning how influence spreads through a social network is difficult when some node activations are never observed. This paper studies whether influence functions can still be learned when observations are randomly missing. That assumption is central to its theoretical results, which establish both proper and improper probably approximately correct learnability.

For discrete-time linear-threshold and independent-cascade models, the proper-learning result transforms incomplete observations into complete observations on a modified graph. Proper learning keeps the learned function within the specified model class. The improper-learning result permits a different representation and also covers the continuous-time independent-cascade model, extending the range of diffusion settings addressed.

The latter result uses features based on reachability and leads to an efficient practical heuristic. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the method can compensate even when a fairly large fraction of observations is missing. The paper thus combines conditional learning guarantees with empirical evidence that the resulting approach can remain useful under substantial observational gaps.
neurips-2016-learning-influence-function.tldr: Influence functions remain PAC-learnable under randomly missing activations for several diffusion models, and a practical method compensates for substantial missing data.

paragraphs: When estimating a network from observations, densely connected groups can be an important part of its structure. GRAB learns both a network among measured variables and the dense groups within that network. It takes a matrix of variables and samples as input, without requiring those groups to be supplied in advance.

A central feature is that the groups, called blocks, can overlap. A variable can therefore participate in more than one densely connected component. The method learns this organization jointly with the network itself. Its optimization uses block coordinate descent, with each individual step forming a convex problem; the abstract makes this stepwise convexity claim rather than a claim that the entire joint problem is convex.

On synthetic data, GRAB recovers underlying network structure substantially better than four state-of-the-art competitors. On cancer gene-expression data, it better reveals known functional gene sets and potentially novel cancer-driving genes. The latter are candidate discoveries, while the recovery of known sets provides evidence that the learned overlapping organization captures biologically relevant structure.
neurips-2016-learning-sparse-gaussian-gr.tldr: GRAB jointly learns a sparse network and overlapping dense groups, improving structural recovery in synthetic and cancer gene-expression studies.

paragraphs: Deep networks often have their layer widths chosen manually. Wide architectures can perform well, but their memory and computation requirements make them difficult to use on constrained platforms. This paper starts from the observation that many network parameters are redundant and asks whether the number of neurons in each layer can instead be determined during learning.

The proposed method applies a group-sparsity regularizer to network parameters, with each group associated with a single neuron. This organizes the pressure toward compactness around whole neurons, making the regularizer relevant to layer width. Training begins with an overcomplete network, allowing the learning procedure to identify a smaller architecture within that starting model.

The authors show parameter reductions of up to 80% while retaining or even improving accuracy. This is a reported attainable reduction, rather than a guarantee for every network. The result supports learning layer widths through neuron-level sparsity as a practical way to obtain compact models without necessarily sacrificing predictive quality.
neurips-2016-learning-the-number-of-neur.tldr: Neuron-level group sparsity learns layer widths during training, reducing parameters by up to 80% while retaining or improving accuracy.

paragraphs: Recursive teaching dimension measures the worst-case number of labeled examples needed to learn a target concept under a particular teaching model. This paper investigates how that quantity relates to VC dimension, another measure of learning complexity. Its goal is to bound teaching complexity using the structural complexity captured by VC dimension.

For a class with VC dimension d, the authors prove that its recursive teaching dimension is at most d × 2^(d+1). The key advance is that this bound depends only on d. Earlier bounds also involved the number of concepts; the new result removes that dependence and is independent of the domain size as well.

The paper also constructs classes with VC dimension 3k and recursive teaching dimension 5k. These examples establish that the worst-case ratio can reach 5/3, exceeding the previously known value of 3/2. Together, the results tighten knowledge from both directions: they provide a universal upper bound in terms of VC dimension and demonstrate a larger possible separation between the two measures.
neurips-2016-on-the-recursive-teaching-d.tldr: The paper bounds recursive teaching dimension solely by VC dimension and constructs classes where their ratio reaches 5/3.

paragraphs: Nonconvex learning methods often work well empirically, but explaining their full optimization trajectory remains difficult. This paper introduces an analysis based on diffusion processes, using stochastic gradient descent for a tensor-decomposition formulation of independent component analysis as its concrete setting. The aim is to describe how the algorithm moves toward a desirable local minimum over time.

Starting from an unstable equilibrium, the analyzed dynamics pass through three phases. First, an unstable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process describes a slow departure from initialization. Next, an ordinary differential equation describes rapid movement toward the desirable minimum. Finally, a stable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process describes fluctuations around that minimum.

This phase-by-phase account distinguishes the roles of random fluctuations and systematic motion along the trajectory. The proof uses weak convergence of Markov chains to diffusion processes to connect the discrete optimization algorithm with continuous mathematical descriptions. The result is a detailed analysis for the stated ICA formulation and initialization, providing an analytic approach to understanding nonconvex optimization dynamics.
neurips-2016-online-ica-understanding-gl.tldr: A diffusion-based analysis describes three phases of SGD for tensor-based ICA, from leaving an unstable equilibrium to fluctuating around a desirable minimum.

paragraphs: Hidden count variables can take any nonnegative integer value, giving them infinitely many possible states. That creates a difficulty for standard exact inference methods in graphical models. Common alternatives truncate the range of counts or use sampling approximations, but those choices introduce approximation into the calculations used to learn and reason about the model.

This paper represents factors over countably infinite states with probability generating functions. It then performs variable elimination directly with those functions. The representation makes exact inference possible for the class of latent-count models considered, without replacing the infinite state space with a finite cutoff.

The authors describe the resulting algorithms as exact and pseudo-polynomial in running time, and report that they are much faster than existing approximate techniques. In population-ecology problems, avoiding approximate likelihood calculations leads to better parameter estimates. The significance is therefore both computational and statistical: the representation supports efficient exact calculations whose improved accuracy carries through to the inferred model parameters.
neurips-2016-probabilistic-inference-wit.tldr: Probability generating functions enable fast exact inference for a class of latent-count models and improve parameter estimation in population ecology.

paragraphs: A robot operating in a changing environment needs a map that represents both where obstacles are and how occupancy changes over time. This paper addresses continuous occupancy mapping in dynamic urban settings, where spatial and temporal dependencies make the problem difficult. It formulates mapping as learning a kernel classifier in an efficient feature space.

The central idea incorporates changes over time into the spatial representation. A hierarchical model propagates uncertainty about motion into the kernel. This allows the learned map to predict future occupancy directly from past observations, making the representation relevant to trajectory planning when future obstacle positions are uncertain.

The method retains computational advantages of static Hilbert maps, including fast parameter optimization with stochastic gradient descent and incremental updates as new observations arrive. Experiments at urban road intersections show accurate modeling of map changes and advantages over other techniques on several aspects. These findings support combining temporal prediction, motion uncertainty, and incremental learning within a continuous occupancy representation.
neurips-2016-spatio-temporal-hilbert-map.tldr: Spatio-temporal Hilbert maps incorporate motion uncertainty to learn continuous dynamic maps and predict future occupancy from past observations.

paragraphs: Graphs can contain meaningful patterns at several scales, as illustrated by molecular graphs. A similarity measure focused only on local neighborhoods or only on the whole graph can miss this layered organization. The Multiscale Laplacian Graph kernel addresses the problem by constructing a hierarchy of nested subgraphs and accounting for structure across that hierarchy.

Its main building block is the Feature Space Laplacian Graph kernel. This kernel converts a base similarity measure between vertices into a similarity measure between graphs. The multiscale construction applies that operation recursively to subgraphs, allowing comparisons at different levels to contribute to the overall representation of graph similarity.

The paper also introduces a randomized projection procedure to make the construction computationally feasible. It resembles the Nyström method but operates on reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space operators. The contribution combines a way to represent graph structure at multiple scales with a computational mechanism for using it, addressing both the scope of the comparison and the cost of carrying it out.
neurips-2016-the-multiscale-laplacian-gr.tldr: The Multiscale Laplacian Graph kernel recursively compares nested subgraphs to capture structure across scales, using randomized projection for computational feasibility.

paragraphs: Exact Gaussian-process inference becomes prohibitively expensive for large datasets, making sparse approximations important for practical use. This paper examines two popular approaches for regression: the Fully Independent Training Conditional approximation and the Variational Free Energy approximation. The central question is how their apparent resemblance relates to their actual mathematical and practical behavior.

The authors investigate both methods analytically and through illustrative examples. The analytical component examines their theoretical properties, while the examples show how differences appear in practice. This combination matters because an approximation is judged not only by its formulation but also by the behavior it produces when used for regression.

The study finds that the two methods have surprisingly different theoretical properties and practical behavior despite their superficial similarities. It draws conclusions intended to guide their application. The paper’s contribution is a comparative understanding of established approximations: it explains why treating them as interchangeable on the basis of resemblance would overlook distinctions relevant to practical Gaussian-process inference.
neurips-2016-understanding-probabilistic.tldr: An analytical and illustrative comparison shows that FITC and VFE sparse Gaussian-process approximations differ substantially despite their apparent similarities.

paragraphs: Boltzmann machines can represent complex distributions with multiple modes and structure at different scales. Their parameters are usually learned by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence between the training data and the model distribution. This paper proposes a different training objective that incorporates a meaningful distance between individual observations.

The approach assumes that this observation-level metric is known. It uses the metric to define a Wasserstein distance between the distribution represented by the model and the distribution given by the training sample. The authors derive a gradient of this distance with respect to model parameters, providing a way to optimize the proposed objective.

Training with the new objective yields generative models with different statistical properties. The authors demonstrate their practical potential on data completion and denoising, tasks where the metric between observations plays a crucial role. The contribution connects the chosen notion of similarity in data space with the objective used to fit a generative model, and shows applications in which that connection is useful.
neurips-2016-wasserstein-training-of-res.tldr: Wasserstein training uses a known metric between observations to fit Boltzmann machines, with demonstrated potential for completion and denoising.
